To: Renters Board / Notices
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: DRAFT — STOP USING Brightline Pro 6% developer, batch LX2291

DRAFT FOR REVIEW — NOT TO BE POSTED YET

Please check your developer before your next client. Kelvin Trade has confirmed a filling error affecting Brightline Pro 6% (20 vol) Cream Developer 1L, batch LX2291. Bottles labelled 6% may actually contain 12% (40 vol) — twice the labelled strength.

This is a safety warning, not just a returns notice. A client had burning and visible scalp redness during my bleach service on Saturday using a bottle from this batch. Please don’t assume it’s fine because you’ve used the same mix for years.

WHICH BOTTLES TO CHECK

The affected batch is LX2291, supplied between 19 October and 5 November 2026.

Check the BASE OF EACH BOTTLE. The batch number isn’t on the box, so checking the outer packaging won’t do. Check open bottles in your trolley as well as unopened stock in the back, including anything bought from the Kelvin Trade rep.

Kelvin Trade says other batches and other strengths aren’t affected. If the code is missing or unreadable, put the bottle aside and ask them to confirm before using it. Don’t guess.

IF YOU FIND LX2291

Stop using it immediately. Mark it clearly “DO NOT USE” and keep it separate from usable stock. Don’t try to dilute it, adjust your mixing ratio or use it up on a different service.

The rep is in Tuesday, so bottles can go back to him, or be taken to the Hillington depot, for full credit.

If you’ve had a problem with a bottle, KEEP THAT BOTTLE BACK, with its remaining contents and label intact. Don’t bin it or hand it back with the routine returns before checking what your insurer needs. Keep it securely out of use. Take photos of the label and batch code, and keep the supplier email, purchase details and dated service notes. Keep any client details and photos private, not on this board.

WHAT IT CAN DO TO THE HAIR AND SCALP

A stronger developer can make the bleach mixture work much faster and more aggressively than expected. That can mean excess heat, uneven lift, dryness, weakened hair or breakage, as well as scalp irritation or chemical burns.

On Saturday, lift was much faster than normal before the client reported burning. There’s also been a separate report involving LX2291 of unusually hot foils and rapid, patchy lift. Those signs aren’t proof of the strength in any individual bottle, but they mustn’t be brushed off as just the heater or normal processing.

A patch test doesn’t establish the developer’s strength or make this batch safe.

IF SOMEONE REACTS IN THE CHAIR

Stop the service immediately. Don’t wait for the timer, and don’t tell them to sit through burning.

For a suspected chemical burn:
• Call 999 for medical help immediately. Don’t wait for blistering or severe pain.
• Wear gloves. Carefully remove foils and contaminated clothing where possible without spreading the product.
• Rinse the affected area with plenty of cool or lukewarm running water for about one hour. Have someone make the call while rinsing starts, and follow the call handler’s instructions.
• Don’t use shampoo, creams, aloe or other chemicals, and don’t try to neutralise it.
• Chemical burns need hospital assessment. Breathing difficulty, throat swelling or collapse also mean 999 immediately.

Once urgent care is underway, record what happened in the incident book at the desk and keep dated notes of the products, batch, mix, timings and symptoms. No further colour or bleach on an injured scalp.

This follows the chemical-burn guidance in our “Patch tests and skin tests” page and the NHS reference:
https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acid-and-chemical-burns/

Please make sure everyone renting here sees this before mixing up. A burnt scalp is not an “inconvenience”.

Kirsty
